title: Covalent bonds and Lewis formulas
html:
Guiding question

What determines the covalent nature and properties of a substance?

This is the largest topic in Structure. At SL it covers how covalent bonds form, Lewis formulas, coordination bonds, VSEPR shapes, polarity, giant covalent structures, intermolecular forces and chromatography. At HL it adds resonance, benzene, expanded octets (5 and 6 electron domains), formal charge, sigma and pi bonds, and hybridization. The understandings are numbered S2.2.1–S2.2.16 below.

Starter: two oxygen atoms want two more electrons each. How can they both get them? Think, then reveal

Neither oxygen atom can pull electrons off the other (both are strongly electronegative), so transfer is impossible. Instead each atom shares two of its electrons with the other: two shared pairs, a double bond, O=O. Each O then has a share in eight outer electrons.

Types of bonding: a reminder

BondingBetweenWhat happens to electrons
Ionicmetal + non-metaltransferred
Covalentnon-metals onlyshared in pairs
Metallicmetals onlydelocalized among cations

All three types involve changes to the electrons in the outermost shells of the atoms.

S2.2.1 Covalent bonds and the octet rule

DefinitionA covalent bond is the electrostatic attraction between a shared pair of electrons and the positively charged nuclei of the two bonded atoms.

Covalent bonds form between non-metal atoms, which all have fairly high electronegativities, so neither atom can remove an electron from the other. By sharing, each atom gains a share of extra electrons. The octet rule says atoms tend to share electrons until each has eight electrons in its valence shell (a noble gas configuration). Hydrogen is the exception: it needs only two (like helium).

Example: Cl₂. Each Cl atom (2,8,7; 3s² 3p⁵) needs one more electron. The two atoms share one pair, giving each a full octet. One shared pair = one single bond, drawn as Cl–Cl.

Lewis formulas

A Lewis formula (electron dot structure) shows all the valence electrons in a molecule or ion: bonding pairs and lone pairs (non-bonding pairs). Electrons can be shown as dots, crosses, or a line for each pair. Both the "full" dot-and-cross version and the "line" version (bonds as lines, lone pairs as dots or lines) earn full marks in IB.

  1. Count the total valence electrons (add one per negative charge, subtract one per positive charge).
  2. Put the least electronegative atom in the centre (never H). Join the atoms with single bonds.
  3. Complete the octets of the outer atoms with lone pairs, then put any remaining electrons on the central atom.
  4. If the central atom lacks an octet, move lone pairs from outer atoms to make double or triple bonds.
  5. For ions, draw square brackets and write the charge outside.
Worked example · Lewis formulas of simple moleculesH₂O: 6 + 2 = 8 valence e⁻ → 2 O–H bonds + 2 lone pairs on O
NH₃: 5 + 3 = 8 → 3 N–H bonds + 1 lone pair on N
CH₄: 4 + 4 = 8 → 4 C–H bonds, no lone pairs
CO₂: 4 + 12 = 16 → O=C=O, 2 lone pairs on each O
HCN: 1 + 4 + 5 = 10 → H–C≡N, 1 lone pair on N
NH₄⁺: 5 + 4 − 1 = 8 → 4 N–H bonds, in brackets with + charge

How many valence electrons must be shown in the Lewis formula of the carbonate ion, CO₃²⁻?

C 4 + 3 × O 6 = 22, plus 2 for the 2− charge = 24. That is 12 pairs: one C=O, two C–O, and lone pairs to complete every octet (with the ion in brackets and 2− outside).

Exam tipLone pairs on every atom (including the outer F, Cl or O atoms) must be shown in a Lewis formula. Missing lone pairs is the most common way marks are lost. Hydrogen is never the central atom and never has a lone pair.
Plenary: draw Lewis formulas for HF, H₂S, C₂H₆ and CH₃CH₂COOH, then reveal
  • HF: H–F with three lone pairs on F.
  • H₂S: like water: two S–H bonds and two lone pairs on S.
  • C₂H₆: C–C single bond, each C with three C–H bonds; no lone pairs.
  • CH₃CH₂COOH: CH₃–CH₂–C(=O)–O–H; the C=O oxygen has two lone pairs and the O–H oxygen has two lone pairs.

Exceptions to the octet rule (SL)

  • Incomplete octets: Be and B. In BeCl₂, Be has only 4 valence electrons; in BF₃ and BCl₃, B has only 6. These are "electron deficient" and can accept a lone pair (see coordination bonds).
  • Expanded octets: atoms in period 3 and below (P, S, Cl, Xe…) can have more than 8 electrons around them, e.g. PCl₅ (10) and SF₆ (12). These are covered at AHL (S2.2.13). Period 2 atoms (C, N, O, F) can never exceed an octet because they have no 2d sublevel; that is why NBr₅ cannot exist.

S2.2.2 Single, double and triple bonds; bond length and strength

Atoms can share one, two or three pairs of electrons: a single bond (2 electrons), a double bond (4 electrons) or a triple bond (6 electrons). O₂ has O=O; N₂ has N≡N with one lone pair on each N (so N₂ has 2 non-bonding pairs in total). Ethene has C=C; ethyne has C≡C.

Key pointThe more electron pairs shared between two atoms, the shorter and stronger the bond. More shared electrons between the nuclei means a greater attraction, pulling the nuclei closer together and needing more energy to break.

Data from the data booklet (values rounded). So C–C bond strength increases C₂H₆ < C₂H₄ < C₂H₂ and bond length decreases in the same order. For carbon–oxygen bonds, the shortest is in CO (triple), then CO₂ (double), then CH₃OH (single).

Bond strength also depends on atom size: down group 17 the H–X bond gets longer and weaker (H–F > H–Cl > H–Br > H–I) because the shared pair is further from the nucleus of the halogen.

Which diatomic molecule has the strongest bond between its atoms?

  1. H₂
  2. N₂
  3. O₂
  4. F₂

N₂ has a triple bond (945 kJ mol⁻¹), much stronger than O=O (498) or the single bonds in H₂ (436) and F₂ (159).

Compared with the carbon–carbon bond in C₂H₄, the carbon–carbon bond in C₂H₂ is…

  1. longer and weaker
  2. longer and stronger
  3. shorter and weaker
  4. shorter and stronger

C₂H₂ has a triple bond (3 shared pairs) and C₂H₄ a double bond (2 pairs). More shared pairs → shorter (120 vs 134 pm) and stronger (839 vs 614 kJ mol⁻¹).

Which compound contains covalent bonds but is classified as ionic?

  1. CH₄
  2. SO₃
  3. (NH₄)₂HPO₄
  4. C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁

Ammonium hydrogenphosphate is made of NH₄⁺ and HPO₄²⁻ ions, so it is ionic, even though the bonds inside each ion are covalent. CH₄, SO₃ and sucrose are molecular covalent.

title: Coordination bonds
html:
S2.2.3 Coordination (dative covalent) bonds

Starter: draw BCl₃. What is surprising about it?

Boron (2,3) forms three B–Cl bonds and ends up with only six electrons around it, not eight. BCl₃ is stable anyway, but the boron has an empty orbital that can accept a pair of electrons from another species. That is the key to coordination bonding.

So far, each atom in a covalent bond has given one electron to the shared pair. Sometimes it is energetically favourable for one species to donate a whole lone pair to another atom or ion that has an empty orbital, so that both end up with full sublevels.

DefinitionA coordination bond (dative covalent bond) is a covalent bond in which both shared electrons come from the same atom. It is drawn as an arrow from the atom donating the lone pair to the atom accepting it.

One species must have a lone pair; the other must have an empty orbital to accept it. Once formed, a coordination bond is identical to any other covalent bond.

  • NH₄⁺: NH₃ donates its lone pair to H⁺. All four N–H bonds are then identical.
  • H₃O⁺: H₂O donates one of its lone pairs to H⁺.
  • CO: C≡O, where two bonds are normal shared pairs and the third is a lone pair donated from O to C. Each atom then has an octet.
  • NH₃BF₃: N on NH₃ donates its lone pair to the electron-deficient B in BF₃ (B gains an octet).
  • Al₂Cl₆: two AlCl₃ units form a dimer; a lone pair on a Cl of each unit is donated to the Al of the other, so each Al gets an octet.
  • Complex ions such as [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺: ligands donate lone pairs to a transition metal ion (more in Reactivity 3.4 and Structure 3.1).
Predict first: in the C≡O arrow notation, which way does the arrow point?

From O to C, because oxygen supplies both electrons of the dative pair. (A common error is to point it from C to O.)

Common mistakeNH₃ itself contains no dative bond; NH₄⁺ does. HCHO and H₂O₂ have no dative bonds; CO and H₃O⁺ do. Exam MCQs often test exactly these.

Which species contains a coordination (dative covalent) bond?

  1. HCN
  2. C₂H₂
  3. CO₂
  4. CO

In CO, one of the three shared pairs comes entirely from O. HCN, C₂H₂ and CO₂ have only ordinary shared-pair bonds.

Ammonia reacts with boron trichloride to form H₃NBCl₃. How is the N–B bond formed?

  1. B donates a pair of electrons to N
  2. N donates its lone pair to B
  3. Each atom gives one electron
  4. An electron is transferred from B to N, forming ions

The lone pair on N(H₃) is donated to B(Cl₃), which has an empty orbital. Mark schemes need the direction: "electron pair on N donated to B".

Exam-style: state the type of bond formed between PH₃ and H⁺, and how it forms [2]

Coordinate / dative covalent bond; the lone pair on P (of PH₃) is donated to H⁺. The product is PH₄⁺. A generic description ("both electrons come from one atom") without naming P and H⁺ does not get the second mark.

Exam-style: AlCl₃ reacts with a chloride ion to form AlCl₄⁻. Name the bond formed and explain how it forms [2]

Coordinate (dative) bond. A lone pair on the Cl⁻ ion is donated to the Al of AlCl₃ (which has only six outer electrons). Saying "from Cl" rather than "from Cl⁻" was penalised.

Fill the gaps: for a coordination bond, the donor needs a lone pair and the acceptor needs an empty orbital.

Challenge (HL flavour): can H₂O, H₂S, PCl₃ and PCl₅ each form a coordinate bond with H⁺?

H₂O yes (two lone pairs on O; gives H₃O⁺). H₂S yes, weakly (lone pairs on S; gives H₃S⁺, much less readily). PCl₃ has a lone pair on P, so in principle yes. PCl₅ has no lone pair on P (all five pairs are bonding), so it cannot act as a lone-pair donor through P.

title: VSEPR: shapes of molecules
html:
S2.2.4 VSEPR theory: shapes and bond angles

We usually draw molecules flat on paper, but very few molecules are flat. Methane, for example, is a tetrahedron. Wedge-and-dash drawings show 3D: a solid wedge comes towards you, a dashed wedge goes away from you.

The valence shell electron pair repulsion (VSEPR) model predicts molecular shapes:

  1. Electron domains around the central atom repel each other.
  2. They arrange themselves as far apart as possible to minimize repulsion.
  3. Lone pairs repel more strongly than bonding pairs, because they are held closer to the central nucleus and spread out more.
Repulsion: lone pair–lone pair > lone pair–bonding pair > bonding pair–bonding pair

An electron domain is any region of electron density around the central atom: a lone pair, a single bond, a double bond or a triple bond. A multiple bond counts as one domain. (CO₂ has four bonding pairs but only two domains, so it is linear.)

Method (do not skip step 1, short-cuts lead to silly mistakes):

  1. Draw the Lewis formula.
  2. Count electron domains around the central atom → electron domain geometry.
  3. Count how many are lone pairs → molecular geometry (the shape describes the positions of atoms only).
  4. Each lone pair squeezes the bond angles by roughly 2–2.5°.

2. 4 electron domains → tetrahedral
3. No lone pairs → molecular geometry tetrahedral

2. 4 electron domains → tetrahedral electron domain geometry
3. 1 lone pair → molecular geometry trigonal pyramidal
4. Lone pair repels more than bonding pairs → angle reduced from 109.5° to ≈107°

Your go: what is the H–O–H bond angle in water, in degrees?

Four electron domains (2 bonding, 2 lone pairs) → tetrahedral electron domain geometry; two lone pairs repel more strongly, squeezing the angle from 109.5° by about 2.5° each to 104.5°. Shape: bent (V-shaped).

Exam tip"Explain the bond angle" answers need: number of electron domains, the lone pair(s), and that lone pairs repel more strongly so the bonding pairs are pushed closer. The angles in CH₄, NH₃ and H₂O therefore decrease: CH₄ (109.5°) > NH₃ (107°) > H₂O (104.5°). CH₄ and NH₄⁺ have the same angle; so do NH₃ and H₃O⁺.

In larger molecules, apply VSEPR to each central atom separately. In ethene each C has three domains (120°); in chloroethene the H–C–Cl angle is ≈120°. In hydrazine, N₂H₄, each N has three bonds and a lone pair (≈107°). In N₂H₆²⁺, each N has four bonds and no lone pair (109.5°).

Which species contains a bond angle of approximately 107°?

  1. H₂O
  2. CF₄
  3. NCl₃
  4. BF₃

NCl₃ has 3 bonding pairs and 1 lone pair on N: trigonal pyramidal, ≈107°. H₂O ≈104.5°, CF₄ 109.5°, BF₃ 120°.

What are the shape and bond angle of BF₃?

  1. trigonal pyramidal, 107°
  2. trigonal planar, 120°
  3. tetrahedral, 109.5°
  4. T-shaped, 90°

B has three bonding domains and no lone pair (only 6 electrons), so trigonal planar, 120°.

Which pair has the same bond angles?

  1. CH₄ and NH₄⁺
  2. NH₃ and H₂O
  3. C₂H₄ and C₂H₂
  4. CO₂ and SO₂

CH₄ and NH₄⁺ both have four bonding pairs and no lone pairs: 109.5°. SO₂ is bent (lone pair on S) while CO₂ is linear.

BF₃ and NF₃ have similar formulas but different shapes. Explain why

In BF₃, B has 3 valence electrons, forms three bonds and has no lone pair: 3 domains → trigonal planar, 120°. In NF₃, N has 5 valence electrons, forms three bonds and keeps one lone pair: 4 domains → trigonal pyramidal, about 102–107°. The lone pair makes the difference.

Predict the shape and O–N–O angle of the nitrite ion, NO₂⁻, and say whether it is polar

Valence electrons 5 + 12 + 1 = 18. Lewis: O=N–O⁻ with one lone pair on N. Domains on N: 2 bonding + 1 lone pair = 3 → trigonal planar electron domain geometry; shape bent, angle slightly less than 120° (≈117°). The N–O bonds are polar and the shape is asymmetric, so the ion is polar (net dipole).

SiCl₄: how many outer electrons does Si have, how many after bonding, how many pairs, and what shape?

Si has 4 outer electrons; after forming four Si–Cl bonds it has a share of 8; that is 4 pairs, all bonding (no lone pairs), so SiCl₄ is tetrahedral, 109.5°.

title: Bond polarity and molecular polarity
html:
S2.2.5 Bond polarity and electronegativity

DefinitionElectronegativity is the ability of an atom to attract a shared pair of electrons (the electron density of a covalent bond) towards itself. It is measured on the Pauling scale (F = 4.0, the highest). Noble gases have no value.

When electrons are thought of as clouds of charge, electron density describes how that charge is spread out. Electronegativity depends on: (1) nuclear charge, (2) atomic radius (distance from nucleus to the bonding electrons), and (3) shielding by inner electrons.

  • Across a period it increases: nuclear charge increases while shielding stays about the same, so the atomic radius decreases and the bonding pair is attracted more strongly.
  • Down a group it decreases: the atomic radius and shielding increase, so the bonding pair is further from the nucleus and attracted less strongly, despite the larger nuclear charge.
Model answer: state and explain the trend in electronegativity across period 3 from Na to S [4]
  • Electronegativity increases across the period;
  • nuclear charge (proton number) increases;
  • the number of shells stays the same, so shielding is about the same (and the atomic radius decreases);
  • so the attraction of the nucleus for the bonding pair increases.

Note that electronegativity is about attracting a shared bonding pair, not about removing an electron. Do not explain it with ionization energy.

Most electronegative atoms (data booklet values): F (4.0) > O (3.4) > Cl (3.2) ≈ N (3.0). Of these, only F, O and N form hydrogen bonds: they combine high electronegativity with small atoms carrying lone pairs.

If two bonded atoms have the same electronegativity (Cl–Cl), the electrons are shared equally and the bond is non-polar. If they differ (H–Cl), the more electronegative atom pulls the pair towards itself, gaining a partial negative charge (δ−) and leaving the other atom δ+. The bond is polar and has a bond dipole.

Hδ+–Clδ− (EN: H 2.2, Cl 3.2)

The larger the electronegativity difference, the more polar the bond. Using data booklet values: O–H (Δ ≈ 1.2) is more polar than N–H (≈ 0.8) and C–H (≈ 0.4); C–H is only very slightly polar. Bonding is a continuum: equal sharing → polar covalent → ionic as ΔEN increases.

Using data booklet values (H 2.2, Cl 3.2), what is the electronegativity difference in the H–Cl bond?

3.2 − 2.2 = 1.0. The bond is polar covalent with Cl δ−.

Which bond is the least polar?

  1. C–H
  2. F–H
  3. O–H
  4. N–H

ΔEN: C–H 0.4, N–H 0.8, O–H 1.2, F–H 1.8. C–H is only very slightly polar.

Which single covalent bond is the most polar? (EN: H 2.2, C 2.6, O 3.4, S 2.6)

  1. C–O
  2. S–H
  3. C–H
  4. O–H

O–H has ΔEN = 1.2; C–O 0.8; S–H and C–H 0.4.

S2.2.6 Molecular polarity

A molecule is polar (has a net dipole moment) only if it has polar bonds and its shape is such that the bond dipoles do not cancel. Symmetrical molecules with identical outer atoms and no lone pairs on the central atom are non-polar even if their bonds are polar.

Exam tip"Explain why chloromethane is polar" [2]: Cl is more electronegative than C, so the C–Cl bond is polar; the molecule is asymmetric so the bond dipoles do not cancel and there is a net dipole. For CO₂ say: C=O bonds are polar, but the molecule is linear and symmetrical, so the two dipoles cancel.

Which molecule is non-polar?

  1. CCl₄
  2. CH₂Cl₂

CCl₄ is tetrahedral with four identical C–Cl dipoles that cancel. Replacing any Cl by H breaks the symmetry; CO has a single polar bond.

Fill the gaps: a molecule can contain polar bonds but be non-polar overall if it is symmetrical, so that the bond dipoles cancel.

Practical: polarity of molecules

Practical evidence: a stream of a polar liquid (e.g. water) is deflected by a charged rod; a non-polar liquid (e.g. cyclohexane) is not. In the class microwave practical, polar molecules try to line up with the oscillating field and heat up, while non-polar liquids barely warm. (Ethanol heats faster than water because of its lower specific heat capacity, not because it is more polar.)

Method in brief: heat 10.0 cm³ of water for a short burst (about 10 s) and find the time that raises its temperature by about 40 °C; then give 10.0 cm³ of each other liquid (cyclohexane, methylbenzene, tetrachloromethane, ethanol, propanol, butan-1-ol) exactly the same time and record the temperature rise. Many of the liquids are flammable and some are toxic: keep them away from flames and use a fume cupboard where advised; return uncontaminated liquids to their bottles and put the rest in organic waste.

Reveal: answers to the practical questions
  1. Water vs non-polar liquid: water molecules are polar, so they keep trying to align with the rapidly oscillating field and rotate; this kinetic energy raises the temperature. Non-polar molecules (cyclohexane, CCl₄) have no dipole to be turned, so their temperature barely changes.
  2. Ice heats slowly: the molecules are locked in a hydrogen-bonded lattice and cannot rotate freely.
  3. Ethanol vs water: ethanol is less polar than water, yet its temperature often rises more, because 10 cm³ of ethanol has a smaller mass and a much lower specific heat capacity (≈2.4 vs 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹), so the same energy gives a bigger temperature rise.
  4. Longer alcohols: propanol and butan-1-ol have larger non-polar hydrocarbon parts, so the molecules are less polar overall and heat up less per unit of energy absorbed.

title: Giant covalent structures
html:
S2.2.7 Covalent network (giant covalent) structures

In a covalent network structure, atoms are joined by covalent bonds in a continuous 3D (or 2D) lattice with no discrete molecules. These are LARGE structures (sometimes called macromolecules) containing huge numbers of strong covalent bonds. Breaking the structure means breaking many strong covalent bonds, so these substances have very high melting points and are insoluble in all solvents.

Predict first: will a giant covalent substance have a high or a low melting point? Why?

High. Melting a giant covalent structure means breaking many strong covalent bonds throughout the lattice, which needs a lot of energy (a high temperature). Compare a simple molecular substance, where melting only overcomes weak intermolecular forces.

Allotropes are different structural forms of the same element in the same physical state. They arise from the different ways the atoms can bond to one another. Carbon forms several allotropes.

DiamondGraphiteGrapheneC₆₀ fullerene

Usesjewellery, cutting and drill bitspencils, lubricant, electrodeselectronics, composites (research)drug delivery, catalysts, nanotubes (research)

Diamond

Each carbon atom is covalently bonded to four others in a tetrahedral arrangement extending in three dimensions. All four outer electrons are used in bonding, so there are no free electrons and diamond does not conduct electricity. It is extremely hard and has a very high melting point because a great many strong C–C bonds must be broken. It is, however, an excellent thermal conductor: heat travels as lattice vibrations through the rigid, strongly bonded network.

Graphite and graphene

Each carbon is bonded to three others in flat hexagonal layers, leaving one electron per atom delocalized across the layer. These delocalized electrons let graphite conduct electricity along (parallel to) the layers, not between them. The layers are held together only by weak London forces, so they slide over each other and flake off (soft, slippery, marks paper). Graphene is a single layer of graphite: one atom thick, extremely strong for its mass, flexible, nearly transparent and an excellent conductor.

Fullerenes and nanotubes

C₆₀ (buckminsterfullerene) is a ball of 60 carbon atoms arranged in hexagons and pentagons, discovered in 1985 by Kroto, Curl and Smalley (Nobel Prize 1996) and named after the architect Buckminster Fuller, whose geodesic domes have the same shape. Unlike the other allotropes it is a simple molecule. Carbon nanotubes are rolled-up graphene sheets: very strong but light, and able to carry very high current densities. Both are being researched for uses in medicine, electronics and materials.

Silicon and silicon dioxide

Silicon has the same tetrahedral structure as diamond. Silicon dioxide (quartz, sand is an impure form) is a giant 3D lattice in which each Si is bonded to four O atoms tetrahedrally and each O to two Si atoms, with single bonds. The formula SiO₂ is only the ratio; it is not a molecule.

Common mistake"SiO₂ is like CO₂." No: CO₂ is a simple molecule (O=C=O) with weak London forces between molecules, so it is a gas. SiO₂ is a giant covalent network with strong Si–O bonds throughout, so it is a high-melting solid. Also, in graphite each carbon forms three single σ bonds plus delocalized electrons, not double bonds.

Which statement about SiO₂ is correct?

  1. It consists of SiO₂ molecules held by London forces
  2. Each Si is bonded to two O atoms by double bonds
  3. Each Si is bonded to four O atoms and each O to two Si atoms
  4. It conducts electricity because it has delocalized electrons

SiO₂ is a giant covalent network: SiO₄ tetrahedra sharing every O between two Si. There are no molecules and no mobile electrons.

Which combination describes silicon and silicon dioxide?

  1. Si: giant covalent, high m.p.; SiO₂: giant covalent, high m.p.
  2. Si: metallic, high m.p.; SiO₂: simple molecular, low m.p.
  3. Si: giant covalent, high m.p.; SiO₂: simple molecular, low m.p.
  4. Si: metallic, low m.p.; SiO₂: giant covalent, high m.p.

Both are covalent networks with strong bonds throughout, so both have very high melting points (Si 1414 °C, SiO₂ about 1700 °C).

Compare: describe the similarities between the properties of diamond and silicon dioxide, related to their structure

Both are giant covalent (network) structures in which every atom is held by strong covalent bonds in a tetrahedral 3D arrangement. So both: have very high melting and boiling points (many strong bonds to break); are very hard; are insoluble in water and other solvents; do not conduct electricity (no delocalized electrons or ions).

Exam tip"Explain why the distance between adjacent C atoms within a graphite layer is shorter than between layers" [3]: within a layer, covalent bonds (shared electrons); between layers, weak London (dispersion) forces; covalent bonds are much stronger, so atoms are held much closer.
Exam-style: discuss two uses of graphite (other than as a lubricant) with reference to its layered structure [4]
  • Pencil "lead": the layers separate and flake off onto the paper (weak forces between layers). Saying only "layers slide" is not enough; the idea of layers separating is needed.
  • Electrodes / batteries: mobile delocalized electrons; current flows parallel to the layers.
  • Carbon fibre: bonding within a layer is very strong and the layers are extensive.

Fill the gaps: graphite conducts electricity because each carbon has one delocalized electron; diamond does not, because all four outer electrons are used in covalent bonds.

title: Intermolecular forces
html:
S2.2.8 Intermolecular forces

Starter: which has the highest boiling point, HF, F₂ or CH₃F? How could you decide?

Identify the strongest intermolecular force in each: F₂ has only London forces; CH₃F is polar, so dipole–dipole forces too; HF has H bonded to F, so hydrogen bonding. Boiling points: F₂ 85 K, CH₃F 194 K, HF 293 K (20 °C).

Intermolecular forces (IMFs) are attractions between molecules. They are much weaker than covalent bonds (which are within molecules): do not confuse the two. When a simple molecular substance melts or boils, only the IMFs are overcome; the covalent bonds stay intact.

ForceOriginPresent inRelative strength
London (dispersion)temporary instantaneous dipole induces a dipole in a neighbourall molecules and atomsweakest per molecule (but grows with size)
Dipole–induced dipolea permanent dipole induces a dipole in a nearby non-polar moleculemixtures of polar and non-polar moleculesweak
Dipole–dipoleattraction between permanent dipoles (δ+ end of one molecule to δ− end of another)polar moleculesstronger than London for similar size
Hydrogen bondingH bonded to N, O or F is attracted to a lone pair on N, O or F of another moleculemolecules with N–H, O–H or H–Fstrongest IMF (but still about 10× weaker than a covalent bond)

London, dipole–induced dipole and dipole–dipole forces together are called van der Waals forces.

London (dispersion) forces

London forces. Electrons are constantly moving, so at any instant the electron cloud may be uneven, creating a temporary dipole. (Even a helium atom, with just two electrons, has a temporary dipole whenever both electrons happen to be on one side.) This induces a dipole in a neighbouring particle and the two attract, until the electrons move again. The strength increases with the number of electrons (larger, more polarizable electron clouds) and with surface contact (a long chain has more contact than a compact, branched molecule). So the boiling points of the noble gases and halogens increase down the group, and pentane boils higher than 2,2-dimethylpropane.

Noble gasElectronsBoiling point / °C
He2−269
Ne10−246
Ar18−186
Kr36−153
Xe54−108
Rn86−62
Explain the trend in boiling point of the noble gases

Boiling point increases down the group. The atoms have more electrons, so their electron clouds are larger and more easily distorted; larger temporary (and induced) dipoles form, so London forces get stronger and more energy is needed to separate the atoms.

Dipole–dipole forces

These act between molecules with a permanent overall dipole. In HCl, the δ+ hydrogen of one molecule is attracted to the δ− chlorine of the next. Many molecules can link up in this way, but the forces are still weak compared with covalent bonds.

Hydrogen bonding

Hydrogen bonding. Needs (1) a H atom covalently bonded to a very electronegative atom (N, O or F), making H strongly δ+, and (2) a lone pair on an N, O or F atom of a neighbouring molecule. Draw it as a dashed line from H to the lone pair, with the X–H···Y arrangement in a straight line (≈180°), and show δ+/δ− and lone pairs.

Common mistakeA hydrogen bond is an intermolecular force, not the covalent O–H bond inside a molecule. Molecules like CH₃CHO, CH₃COCH₃ and CH₃OCH₃ contain O but no O–H bond, so they cannot hydrogen bond with each other (though they can accept hydrogen bonds from water). CHCl₃ has no H bonded to N, O or F.

What intermolecular forces exist between water molecules?

  1. Hydrogen bonds only
  2. London forces and dipole–dipole only
  3. London forces, dipole–dipole forces and hydrogen bonds
  4. Covalent bonds and hydrogen bonds

All molecules have London forces; water is polar (dipole–dipole); and it has O–H bonds and lone pairs on O (hydrogen bonds, the strongest). Covalent bonds are inside molecules, not between them.

Which process involves breaking hydrogen bonds?

  1. 2HI(g) → H₂(g) + I₂(g)
  2. CH₄(g) → C(g) + 4H(g)
  3. H₂(l) → H₂(g)
  4. NH₃(l) → NH₃(g)

Boiling ammonia separates molecules held by hydrogen bonds. A and B break covalent bonds; boiling H₂ overcomes only London forces.

Which intermolecular forces are present in liquid hydrogen iodide, HI(l)?

  1. London forces only
  2. London and dipole–dipole forces
  3. Hydrogen bonding
  4. Dipole–dipole forces only

HI is slightly polar (I 2.7, H 2.2), so dipole–dipole forces act as well as London forces (which are the bigger contribution here, given iodine's many electrons). I is not N, O or F, so no hydrogen bonding.

Worksheet: name the strongest IMF in N₂, CCl₄, H₂S, SO, N₂H₂, BH₃, CH₂O and SiH₂O
  • N₂: London
  • CCl₄: London (non-polar)
  • H₂S: dipole–dipole
  • SO (sulfur monoxide): dipole–dipole
  • N₂H₂: hydrogen bonding (N–H)
  • BH₃: London (non-polar, trigonal planar)
  • CH₂O (methanal): dipole–dipole. It contains O but no O–H bond, so it cannot hydrogen bond with itself.
  • SiH₂O: dipole–dipole
Exam-style: explain how hydrogen bonding arises in liquid HF [3]
  • Large electronegativity difference between H and F (F is much more electronegative);
  • so the H–F bond is polar: Hδ+–Fδ−;
  • attraction between the δ+ H of one molecule and a lone pair on F of another molecule.

title: Intermolecular forces and physical properties
html:
S2.2.9 Intermolecular forces and physical properties

Boiling and melting points. The stronger the IMFs, the more energy needed to separate molecules, so the higher the b.p. and enthalpy of vaporization, and the lower the volatility. Compare like with like:

  1. First identify the strongest IMF in each substance.
  2. If the type is the same, compare the number of electrons (molar mass) and shape.
Worked example · Ethanol vs methoxymethaneBoth are C₂H₆O (M = 46.08), but ethanol boils at 78 °C and methoxymethane at −24 °C.
Same number of electrons → similar London forces
Ethanol has an O–H group → hydrogen bonding between molecules
Methoxymethane has no O–H → only dipole–dipole + London
Hydrogen bonds are stronger → more energy needed → higher b.p. for ethanol

Hydrides of groups 14–17

Hydrides of groups 14–17. CH₄ → SnH₄ boiling points rise smoothly with size (London forces only). NH₃, H₂O and HF have anomalously high boiling points compared with the next hydride down (PH₃, H₂S, HCl) because they form hydrogen bonds. Water is highest because each molecule has two H atoms and two lone pairs, so it can take part in up to four hydrogen bonds, more than NH₃ (one lone pair) or HF (one H).

Group 14b.p. / °CGroup 15b.p. / °CGroup 16b.p. / °CGroup 17b.p. / °C
CH₄−162NH₃−33H₂O100HF20
SiH₄−112PH₃−88H₂S−60HCl−85
GeH₄−88AsH₃−62H₂Se−41HBr−67
SnH₄−52SbH₃−17H₂Te−2HI−35

Other examples worth knowing. Order of increasing b.p.: C₂H₆ < HCHO < CH₃OH (London < dipole–dipole < hydrogen bonding). CH₄ < SiH₄ < CH₃Cl < CH₃OH. Methanol boils higher than chloromethane even though it has a lower molar mass (hydrogen bonding).

What is the correct order of increasing boiling point?

  1. C₂H₆ < HCHO < CH₃OH
  2. HCHO < C₂H₆ < CH₃OH
  3. CH₃OH < HCHO < C₂H₆
  4. C₂H₆ < CH₃OH < HCHO

All have similar numbers of electrons. C₂H₆: London only; HCHO: polar, dipole–dipole; CH₃OH: hydrogen bonding.

Exam-style: methanol has a lower molar mass than chloromethane. Explain why its boiling point is higher [2]

Methanol has hydrogen bonding between molecules (O–H group); these are stronger than the dipole–dipole / London forces in chloromethane, so more energy is needed to separate methanol molecules.

The boiling points of PH₃, AsH₃ and SbH₃ increase in that order. What is the main reason?

  1. Hydrogen bonding increases
  2. The molecules become more polar
  3. London forces increase with the number of electrons
  4. Covalent bonds become stronger

More electrons → larger, more polarizable electron clouds → stronger London forces. These hydrides do not hydrogen bond, and boiling does not break covalent bonds. (NH₃ is anomalously high because it does hydrogen bond.)

Solubility

Solubility. "Like dissolves like". Polar and hydrogen-bonding substances (small alcohols, sugars, NH₃) dissolve in water because they can form hydrogen bonds or dipole interactions with water molecules. Non-polar substances (hydrocarbons, I₂) dissolve in non-polar solvents like hexane but not in water. Solubility of alcohols in water falls as the non-polar hydrocarbon chain gets longer.

Exam-style: which of (CH₃)₂NH and CH₄ can form hydrogen bonds with water? Explain [2]

(CH₃)₂NH. It has a hydrogen bonded to nitrogen (N–H, polar) and a lone pair on N, so it can form hydrogen bonds with water: N–H···O and O–H···N. CH₄ has no H bonded to N, O or F and no lone pair.

Electrical conductivity

Electrical conductivity. Simple molecular substances do not conduct in any state because they have no mobile charged particles (no ions or delocalized electrons). Exception: some, like HCl, react with water to form ions, so their solutions conduct.

Structure typeMelting pointConducts?Soluble in water?
Giant ionichighonly molten or aqueousoften
Simple molecularlownoif polar / H-bonding
Giant covalentvery highno (except graphite, graphene)no
Metallicusually highyes, solid and liquidno

A substance melts at 115 °C, does not conduct as a solid or liquid and dissolves in hexane but not water. What is its structure?

  1. Giant ionic
  2. Simple molecular, non-polar
  3. Giant covalent
  4. Metallic

Low melting point and no conduction in any state → simple molecular. Soluble in non-polar hexane but not water → non-polar (this fits sulfur, S₈).

Exam-style: explain why sodium oxide and phosphorus(V) oxide have very different melting points [6]
  • Na and O have a large electronegativity difference → ionic bonding; P and O a smaller difference → covalent bonding.
  • Na₂O is a giant ionic lattice…
  • …with strong electrostatic attractions between oppositely charged ions.
  • P₄O₁₀ is covalent and molecular (simple molecules)…
  • …with only weak intermolecular forces between the molecules.
  • So the melting point of Na₂O is much higher than that of P₄O₁₀.

Practical: boiling points of liquid mixtures

Class practical (boiling points of mixtures). Propan-1-ol/propan-2-ol gives an almost straight-line plot of b.p. against composition because both liquids hydrogen bond, so the forces in the mixture are similar. Ethanol/cyclohexane dips below both pure b.p. values because the mixture breaks up ethanol's hydrogen bonds and only weaker forces remain. Trichloromethane/ethyl ethanoate (or propanone) rises above both because new attractions form between the δ+ H of CHCl₃ and the δ− O of the other liquid.

Method: heat 10 cm³ of one pure liquid under reflux with the thermometer in the liquid and record its boiling point; add the second liquid in 2 cm³ portions down the condenser (flame moved away first), recording the boiling point after each addition; repeat starting from the other liquid. The liquids are volatile and most are highly flammable: use a small flame kept well away when adding liquid, use a fume cupboard for trichloromethane, and put residues in organic waste.

From the example results, by how many °C does the maximum boiling point of the trichloromethane/propanone mixture (67.5 °C) exceed the boiling point of pure trichloromethane (61.2 °C)?

67.5 − 61.2 = 6.3 °C. A rise above both pure liquids is the signature of stronger attractions between unlike molecules.

Sketch the graph you would expect for CHCl₃ and CH₃COCH₃, then reveal

A curve with a maximum above both pure boiling points (see the trichloromethane/propanone results above), because the new C–H···O=C attractions between unlike molecules are stronger than the forces in the pure liquids.

title: Chromatography
html:
S2.2.10 Chromatography

The coloured coating of a sweet, or the ink in a black pen, is usually a mixture of dyes. Chromatography separates the components of a mixture according to how they distribute between a stationary phase and a mobile phase.

  • Paper chromatography: stationary phase is water held in the cellulose fibres of the paper; mobile phase is the solvent.
  • Thin-layer chromatography (TLC): stationary phase is a thin layer of silica (SiO₂) or alumina on a plate; mobile phase is a solvent. TLC is faster and gives sharper separation.

Components continually adsorb onto the stationary phase (stick to its surface by intermolecular forces) and dissolve back into the mobile phase, in a constant dynamic equilibrium. A component that forms stronger intermolecular forces with the stationary phase spends more time stuck and travels a shorter distance. A component that is more soluble in (more attracted to) the mobile phase travels further. With polar silica or paper, polar components move least; with a non-polar solvent, non-polar components move most.

Common mistakeA component with strong intermolecular forces to the stationary phase stays adsorbed longer, so it moves less and has a smaller RF, not a bigger one.

On a silica TLC plate (polar) with a non-polar solvent, which component will have the largest RF?

  1. The most polar component
  2. The component that forms hydrogen bonds with silica
  3. The least polar component
  4. All components have the same RF

The least polar component is held least strongly by the polar silica and is most soluble in the non-polar mobile phase, so it travels furthest.

RF = distance travelled by the component ÷ distance travelled by the solvent front

RF is always between 0 and 1 and has no units. Under the same conditions (same stationary phase, solvent and temperature), a substance always has the same RF, so components can be identified by comparing with standards. Colourless spots are located with UV light or a developing agent (e.g. ninhydrin for amino acids, iodine vapour).

Worked example · RF valueA spot moves 3.6 cm while the solvent front moves 8.0 cm. RF = 3.6 ÷ 8.0 = 0.45

A dye moves 2.8 cm from the start line while the solvent front moves 8.2 cm. Calculate its RF to two significant figures.

RF = 2.8 ÷ 8.2 = 0.341… = 0.34 (no units).

Dye D has an RF of 0.80. The solvent front moved 8.2 cm. How far did dye D move?

distance = RF × solvent distance = 0.80 × 8.2 = 6.6 cm.

Practical tipsDraw the baseline in pencil (ink would itself separate). Keep the baseline above the solvent level so the spots do not dissolve into the solvent reservoir. Cover the tank so the atmosphere is saturated with solvent vapour. Mark the solvent front immediately on removing the paper. In the class "stolen cup" investigation, the culprit's pen is identified by matching the number of spots and their RF values with the ransom-note ink.
Reveal the two mistakes and what problem each causes
  1. The water level is above the start line: the food colours dissolve into the water in the tank instead of travelling up the paper.
  2. The start line is drawn in ink: the ink would itself dissolve and run up the paper, adding extra spots.
Exam-style: explain how the dyes in X are separated by paper chromatography [4]
  • The solvent (mobile phase) moves up through the paper;
  • the dyes have different solubilities in the solvent;
  • and different attractions to the paper (stationary phase);
  • so they are carried different distances in the same time.

Fill the gaps: the RF value has no units and is always between 0 and 1.

Beyond the exam. Forensic scientists use chromatography to match inks and identify substances at crime scenes, and food scientists use it to identify dyes and measure pigments (for example, comparing the vitamin A precursors in different varieties of cassava). DNA profiling uses a related idea, gel electrophoresis, where fragments are separated through a gel by an electric field.

title: Resonance and benzene (AHL)
html:
S2.2.11 Resonance structures AHL

Some molecules and ions cannot be described by a single Lewis formula because a double bond could be placed in more than one equivalent position. Each possible formula is a resonance structure; the real structure is a resonance hybrid, an average of them.

DefinitionResonance occurs when two or more valid Lewis formulas can be drawn for a species, differing only in the position of electrons (not atoms). The pi electrons are delocalized: spread over more than two nuclei rather than fixed between one pair of atoms.

Resonance structures are drawn with a double-headed arrow ↔ between them. The hybrid is drawn with dashed lines for the partial bonds. Important: the molecule does not flip between the forms; the hybrid is a single, unchanging structure.

SpeciesResonance structuresBond orderConsequence
CO₃²⁻31⅓ for each C–Oall three C–O bonds equal length; charge spread over three O atoms
NO₃⁻31⅓all N–O bonds equal
O₃21½both O–O bonds equal, between O–O (H₂O₂) and O=O (O₂) in length
NO₂⁻, SO₂21½both bonds equal
RCOO⁻ (e.g. CH₃COO⁻)21½both C–O bonds equal; charge spread over two O
C₆H₆21½all C–C bonds equal (see S2.2.12)
Bond order = (total number of shared electron pairs between the atoms in all positions) ÷ (number of bond positions)

What is the bond order of each N–O bond in the nitrate ion, NO₃⁻? (Give a decimal to 2 d.p.)

Shared pairs between N and the three O atoms: one double (2) + two single (1 + 1) = 4 pairs over 3 positions. 4 ÷ 3 = 1.33 (1⅓).

Exam tip"Describe the delocalization of π electrons and explain how it accounts for the structure and stability of CO₃²⁻" [3]: π electrons spread over more than two nuclei (all four atoms); all C–O bonds have equal order, length and strength, and the 2− charge is shared equally by the three O atoms; delocalization lowers the energy, so the ion is more stable.

Species without resonance include NH₄⁺, CH₃CH₂O⁻, CH₃COCH₃ (the C=O position is fixed), CO, HCN, CO₂ and C₂H₂.

Which species does NOT have resonance structures?

  1. C₆H₆
  2. NH₄⁺
  3. CO₃²⁻
  4. O₃

NH₄⁺ has four N–H single bonds and no π electrons to delocalize. Benzene, carbonate and ozone all have a double bond that can be drawn in more than one equivalent position.

Which species have delocalized π electrons? I. CH₃COCH₃ II. NO₂⁻ III. CO₃²⁻

  1. I and II only
  2. I and III only
  3. II and III only
  4. I, II and III

In propanone the C=O can only be in one place. NO₂⁻ (2 resonance forms) and CO₃²⁻ (3 forms) have delocalized π electrons.

Ozone: state its shape and bond angle, the hybridization of the central O, and why both O–O bonds are the same length

Bent (V-shaped), about 117° (just under 120°, one lone pair on the central O). Central O is sp². In one Lewis structure there is one O–O (σ only) and one O=O (σ + π), but ozone is a resonance hybrid with a delocalized π bond, so both bonds are identical: bond order 1½, length intermediate between O–O in H₂O₂ and O=O in O₂.

True or false: a pair of structures that differ in where the atoms are (not just the electrons) are resonance structures

False. Resonance structures have identical atom positions; only electrons (π bonds and lone pairs) are moved. Moving atoms gives isomers, not resonance structures.

S2.2.12 Benzene AHL

Benzene, C₆H₆ (empirical formula CH), was isolated by Faraday in 1825. Kekulé proposed (1865, reportedly after dreaming of a snake biting its own tail) a ring of six carbons with alternating single and double bonds (cyclohexa-1,3,5-triene). Three pieces of evidence show this model is wrong:

Faraday's hydrocarbon is 92.3% carbon and 7.7% hydrogen by mass, with Mr = 78. How many carbon atoms are in one molecule?

C: 92.3 ÷ 12.01 = 7.69; H: 7.7 ÷ 1.01 = 7.6. Ratio ≈ 1 : 1, so the empirical formula is CH (M = 13.02). 78 ÷ 13.02 = 6, so the molecular formula is C₆H₆: 6 carbon atoms. Such a low H : C ratio suggested several multiple bonds.

  1. Bond lengths. X-ray diffraction shows all six C–C bonds are the same length, 140 pm, between C–C (154 pm) and C=C (134 pm). Kekulé's structure would be a distorted hexagon.
  2. Thermochemistry. Hydrogenation of cyclohexene releases 120 kJ mol⁻¹, so three C=C bonds should release about 360 kJ mol⁻¹. Benzene releases only about 208 kJ mol⁻¹, so it is about 150 kJ mol⁻¹ more stable than expected. This extra stability is the delocalization (resonance) energy.
  3. Reactivity. Alkenes decolourize bromine water by addition. Benzene does not react with bromine water at room temperature and prefers substitution reactions, which keep the ring intact.
  4. Isomers. Only one 1,2-disubstituted isomer exists (e.g. one 1,2-dichlorobenzene). Kekulé's structure predicts two (Cl atoms across a single or a double bond).

Using −120 kJ mol⁻¹ per C=C, how much more stable (in kJ mol⁻¹) is benzene than the Kekulé structure predicts, given ΔH(hydrogenation of benzene) = −208 kJ mol⁻¹?

Predicted: 3 × (−120) = −360 kJ mol⁻¹. Actual: −208. Difference: 360 − 208 = 152 kJ mol⁻¹. (If you use −119 per C=C, you get 357 − 208 = 149; both round to ≈150.)

Current model. Each carbon is sp² hybridized, forming three σ bonds (two C–C, one C–H) at 120°, so the molecule is planar. Each C has one unhybridized p orbital perpendicular to the ring. These six p orbitals overlap sideways all round the ring, forming a continuous delocalized π system (six electrons) above and below the plane. This is drawn as a hexagon with a circle inside. Each C–C bond has a bond order of 1.5.

Key pointBecause the six π electrons are delocalized, there are no localized C=C bonds for bromine to add across, and any addition would destroy the stable delocalized ring. This is why benzene undergoes electrophilic substitution rather than addition (Reactivity 3.4). The older idea that benzene "rapidly flips" between two Kekulé forms is wrong: there is one structure, the delocalized hybrid.
Exam-style: describe the structure of benzene and give two pieces of evidence for it

Structure: planar hexagonal ring of six C atoms, each bonded to one H; all C–C–C angles 120° (sp²); all C–C bonds equal, intermediate between single and double (bond order 1.5); six π electrons delocalized above and below the ring.

Evidence (any two): all C–C bond lengths equal (X-ray/electron density map); enthalpy of hydrogenation much less exothermic than three times that of cyclohexene; only one 1,2-disubstituted isomer; benzene undergoes substitution, not addition, and does not decolourize bromine water.

Which observation is chemical (not physical) evidence that benzene does not contain three localized C=C bonds?

  1. All C–C bonds are 140 pm
  2. It does not decolourize bromine water at room temperature
  3. Its enthalpy of hydrogenation is −208 kJ mol⁻¹
  4. Its STM image is a regular hexagon

Lack of addition with bromine is chemical (reactivity) evidence. Bond lengths and images are physical evidence; the hydrogenation enthalpy is thermochemical evidence.

title: Expanded octets and formal charge (AHL)
html:
S2.2.13 Expanded octets: five and six electron domains AHL

Elements in period 3 and beyond have empty d orbitals of similar energy available, so their central atoms can accommodate 10 or 12 electrons (5 or 6 electron domains). Period 2 elements cannot.

Key pointIn a trigonal bipyramid, lone pairs always go in the equatorial positions (more space: neighbours at 120° rather than 90°). That is why SF₄ is seesaw, ClF₃ is T-shaped and XeF₂ is linear. In an octahedron, two lone pairs go opposite each other (180°), giving square planar XeF₄.
Worked example · SF₄Valence electrons: 6 + 4 × 7 = 34
4 S–F bonds use 8; each F takes 3 lone pairs (24) → 32 used
2 left → 1 lone pair on S
5 domains (4 bonding + 1 lone) → trigonal bipyramidal electron domain geometry
Lone pair equatorial → seesaw; F–S–F angles <120° (equatorial) and <90° (axial–equatorial), squeezed by the lone pair
Worked example · XeF₄Valence electrons: 8 + 4 × 7 = 36

Symmetrical → non-polar

Which species has a square planar molecular geometry?

  1. SF₄
  2. XeF₄
  3. CF₄
  4. PF₄⁺

XeF₄ has 6 domains (4 bonding, 2 lone pairs opposite each other). SF₄ is seesaw; CF₄ and PF₄⁺ are tetrahedral.

Which molecule is trigonal bipyramidal?

  1. PCl₃
  2. SiCl₄
  3. PCl₅
  4. SF₆

PCl₅: five bonding domains, no lone pairs. PCl₃ is trigonal pyramidal, SiCl₄ tetrahedral and SF₆ octahedral.

Work out the shapes and bond angles of PH₄⁺, PF₃, PF₆⁻ and BrF₃
  • PH₄⁺: 5 + 4 − 1 = 8 e⁻, 4 bonding pairs → tetrahedral, 109.5°.
  • PF₃: 3 bonding + 1 lone pair → trigonal pyramidal, about 97–107° (less than 109.5°).
  • PF₆⁻: 6 bonding pairs → octahedral, 90°.
  • BrF₃: 7 + 21 = 28 e⁻; 3 bonds + 2 lone pairs on Br (5 domains), lone pairs equatorial → T-shaped, angles slightly less than 90°.
Exam-style: draw and name the shapes of AsCl₃ and the Cl₃⁺ ion, including lone pairs that affect the shape [4]

AsCl₃: three As–Cl bonds and one lone pair on As → (trigonal) pyramidal. Cl₃⁺: central Cl has 7 − 1 = 6 electrons available: two Cl–Cl bonds and two lone pairs → bent (V-shaped). "Trigonal" is not accepted for the bent ion.

S2.2.14 Formal charge AHL

When more than one Lewis formula is possible (for example, obeying the octet rule versus expanding the octet), formal charge helps decide which is preferred.

DefinitionThe formal charge (FC) is the charge an atom would have if all bonding electrons were shared equally between the bonded atoms, regardless of electronegativity.
FC = V − (L + ½B) where V = valence electrons of the free atom, L = electrons in lone pairs on the atom, B = electrons in bonds to the atom

Equivalent shortcut: FC = valence electrons − (number of lone-pair electrons + number of bonds). The sum of formal charges equals the overall charge of the species.

Choosing the preferred structure:

  1. The structure in which formal charges are closest to zero is preferred.
  2. If charges remain, prefer the structure with the negative formal charge on the more electronegative atom (and any positive charge on the least electronegative atom).
  3. Prefer structures with the least separation of charge.

When comparing resonance structures more generally: more covalent bonds (more complete octets) is better, fewer formal charges is better, and structures that are equivalent contribute equally (as in benzene).

Worked example · Sulfate, SO₄²⁻Structure A (octet): S with 4 single S–O bonds
S: 6 − (0 + 4) = +2; each O: 6 − (6 + 1) = −1 → charges +2, −1, −1, −1, −1
Structure B (expanded octet): S with 2 S=O and 2 S–O
S: 6 − (0 + 6) = 0; O in S=O: 6 − (4 + 2) = 0; O in S–O: −1
→ charges 0, 0, 0, −1, −1 (sum −2 ✓)
Structure B has formal charges closer to zero → preferred

In the octet structure of the bromate(V) ion, BrO₃⁻ (three Br–O single bonds, one lone pair on Br), what is the formal charge on Br?

FC = V − (L + number of bonds) = 7 − (2 + 3) = +2. Each O has 6 lone-pair electrons and 1 bond: 6 − 7 = −1. Sum: +2 − 3 = −1 ✓.

Worked example · Bromate(V), BrO₃⁻Octet structure: three Br–O single bonds, one lone pair on Br
Br: 7 − (2 + 3) = +2
Expanded octet: two Br=O and one Br–O, one lone pair on Br
Br: 7 − (2 + 5) = 0
The expanded-octet structure has FC(Br) = 0 → preferred
Worked example · CO₂ arrangementO=C=O: C 4 − (0 + 4) = 0; each O 6 − (4 + 2) = 0 → all zero
C=O=O (O central, 2 lone pairs on C): middle O 6 − (0 + 4) = +2; C 4 − (4 + 2) = −2; end O 6 − (4 + 2) = 0 → large separated charges
O=C=O is preferred (C central, all FC = 0)

In the structure of the ethanoate ion drawn as CH₃–C(=O)–O⁻, what is the formal charge on the singly bonded oxygen?

That O has three lone pairs (6 electrons) and one bond: 6 − (6 + 1) = −1. The C=O oxygen is 6 − (4 + 2) = 0. The two resonance structures (swapping which O is double bonded) are equivalent, so the real ion has both C–O bonds equal (bond order 1.5) and −½ on each O.

Sulfate: draw all the resonance structures with two S=O bonds. Is any one of them favoured?

There are six equivalent structures (choose which two of the four O atoms carry the double bonds). They have identical formal charges (0 on S, 0 on the two double-bonded O, −1 on the two single-bonded O), so none is favoured: they contribute equally and all four S–O bonds are the same length. The all-single-bond structure (FC on S = +2) is the one that is not favoured.

Common mistakeFormal charge is not the same as oxidation state. Formal charge assumes equal sharing; oxidation state assumes the more electronegative atom takes all the bonding electrons. In SO₄²⁻, the oxidation state of S is +6 but its formal charge in the preferred structure is 0.

Two Lewis structures are drawn for a species. Which one does formal charge analysis prefer?

  1. The one with the most formal charges
  2. The one with formal charges closest to zero
  3. The one with a negative formal charge on the least electronegative atom
  4. The one obeying the octet rule, always

Formal charges as close to zero as possible (with any negative charge on the more electronegative atom). The octet rule is not decisive for period 3 atoms such as S, P, Cl and Br.

title: Sigma and pi bonds, hybridization (AHL)
html:
S2.2.15 Sigma (σ) and pi (π) bonds AHL

Covalent bonds form when atomic orbitals overlap.

  • A sigma (σ) bond forms by axial (head-on) overlap of orbitals along the line joining the two nuclei. Electron density is concentrated between the nuclei. It can form from s–s, s–p, p–p (end-on) or hybrid orbitals.
  • A pi (π) bond forms by sideways overlap of parallel p orbitals. Electron density lies above and below the internuclear axis, with a plane of zero electron density through the nuclei.
Bondσ bondsπ bonds
single10
double11
triple12

A π bond is weaker than a σ bond (less effective sideways overlap), which is why a C=C double bond (614 kJ mol⁻¹) is less than twice as strong as a C–C single bond (346 kJ mol⁻¹), and why alkenes are more reactive than alkanes. A π bond also prevents rotation about the double bond, which causes cis–trans isomerism (Structure 3.2).

Two p orbitals lie parallel to each other (side by side) and overlap. What forms?

  1. a σ bond
  2. a π bond
  3. a hydrogen bond
  4. a coordination bond

Sideways overlap of parallel p orbitals gives a π bond. Head-on overlap (s–s, s–p, end-on p–p, hybrid orbitals) gives σ bonds.

Worked example · Counting σ and π bondsHCN (H–C≡N): σ = 2, π = 2
Propyne CH₃C≡CH: 4 C–H + 2 C–C framework bonds = 6 σ (the triple bond contributes 1 σ + 2 π) → 6 σ, 2 π
Methanal H₂C=O: 3 σ, 1 π
Propenenitrile CH₂=CH–C≡N: 3 C–H + C=C (1σ) + C–C (1σ) + C≡N (1σ) = 6 σ; π = 1 + 2 = 3
Method: every bond line counts as 1 σ; add 1 π per double bond and 2 π per triple bond
Don't forget the hidden bondsIn condensed or skeletal formulas the C–H bonds are not drawn, but they are still σ bonds and must be counted. Propanone, CH₃COCH₃, has 6 C–H + 2 C–C + 1 C=O = 9 σ and 1 π (not 3 σ). A quick check for an open-chain molecule: number of σ bonds = number of atoms − 1.

Glycine, H₂N–CH₂–COOH (molecule G above): how many σ bonds does it contain?

N–H × 2, N–C, C–H × 2, C–C, C=O (1 σ), C–O, O–H: 2 + 1 + 2 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 9 σ, plus 1 π (in C=O). Check: 10 atoms, open chain → 10 − 1 = 9 σ.

Answers for the rest of the practice set
  • A (propanone): 9 σ, 1 π
  • B (2-methylbut-1-ene, C₅H₁₀): 14 σ, 1 π
  • C (H₂SO₄ drawn with two S=O): 6 σ, 2 π
  • D (benzene, Kekulé): 12 σ, 3 π
  • E (buta-1,2-diene, H₂C=C=CH–CH₃): 9 σ, 2 π
  • G (glycine): 9 σ, 1 π
  • I (propyne): 6 σ, 2 π

For the skeletal formulas (F, H, J) add a C–H bond for every unused carbon valence before counting.

How many σ and π bonds are present in hydrogen cyanide, HCN?

  1. 1 σ and 3 π
  2. 2 σ and 2 π
  3. 3 σ and 1 π
  4. 2 σ and 1 π

H–C is 1 σ; C≡N is 1 σ + 2 π. Total 2 σ, 2 π.

How many σ and π bonds are in CH₃CH₂C≡CCH₂COOH?

  1. 13 σ and 5 π
  2. 15 σ and 2 π
  3. 15 σ and 3 π
  4. 15 σ only

C₆H₈O₂ has 16 atoms in an open chain, so 15 σ. π: 2 in C≡C and 1 in C=O = 3.

Ethyne, H–C≡C–H: how many σ and π bonds?

Two C–H σ bonds plus the σ part of C≡C = 3 σ; the triple bond adds 2 π.

S2.2.16 Hybridization AHL

Carbon's ground state is 1s² 2s² 2p², with only two unpaired electrons, yet in CH₄ it forms four identical bonds at 109.5°. Hybridization explains this.

DefinitionHybridization is the mixing of atomic orbitals on the same atom to form a new set of equivalent hybrid orbitals, which have the same energy and are arranged to minimize repulsion.

sp³ (methane). One 2s electron is promoted to the empty 2p orbital (2s¹ 2p³). The 2s and all three 2p orbitals mix to form four equivalent sp³ hybrid orbitals, each with one electron, arranged tetrahedrally. Each overlaps with an H 1s orbital to form four σ bonds.

sp² (ethene). After promotion, the 2s mixes with two 2p orbitals to give three sp² orbitals at 120° in a plane. One 2p orbital is left unhybridized, perpendicular to the plane. Each C uses its sp² orbitals for σ bonds (two to H, one to the other C). The unhybridized p orbitals on the two carbons overlap sideways to form the π bond.

sp (ethyne, CO₂). The 2s mixes with one 2p to give two sp orbitals at 180°. Two unhybridized p orbitals remain at right angles, forming two π bonds (a triple bond in ethyne; two double bonds at the C of CO₂).

Electron domainsHybridizationGeometryUnhybridized p orbitalsExamples (central atom)
4sp³tetrahedral (109.5°)0C in CH₄, diamond; N in NH₃; O in H₂O and CH₃OH; Si and O in SiO₂
3sp²trigonal planar (120°)1C in C₂H₄, graphite, C₆₀, benzene, CO₃²⁻; B in BF₃; central O in O₃
2splinear (180°)2C in C₂H₂, CO₂, HCN
Exam tip (quick rule)Count the atoms bonded to the atom plus its lone pairs (= electron domains): 4 → sp³, 3 → sp², 2 → sp. For carbon: all single bonds → sp³; one double bond → sp²; a triple bond or two double bonds → sp. Hybridization follows from geometry, not the other way round.
Worked example · Hybridization in moleculesBut-2-ene CH₃CH=CHCH₃: C1 sp³, C2 sp²
Propene CH₃CH=CH₂: sp³ and sp² (no sp)
Methanol CH₃OH: C sp³; O sp³ (2 bonds + 2 lone pairs)
Methanal H₂C=O: C sp², with 3 σ and 1 π
N₂H₆²⁺: each N has 4 σ bonds, no lone pair → sp³, 109.5°

What is the hybridization of carbon and oxygen in methanol, CH₃OH?

  1. C sp³, O sp³
  2. C sp³, O sp²
  3. C sp², O sp³
  4. C sp, O sp³

C has 4 attached atoms (sp³); O has 2 attached atoms + 2 lone pairs = 4 (sp³).

Which allotropes of carbon show sp² hybridization? I. diamond II. graphite III. C₆₀

  1. I and II only
  2. I and III only
  3. II and III only
  4. I, II and III

In graphite and C₆₀ each C bonds to three others (sp²). In diamond each C bonds to four (sp³).

Label the hybridization of each carbon in 2-methylbut-1-ene, CH₃CH₂C(=CH₂)CH₃, and in buta-1,2-diene, H₂C=C=CH–CH₃

2-methylbut-1-ene: CH₃ (of ethyl) sp³; CH₂ (of ethyl) sp³ (four single bonds); the C bearing the =CH₂ sp²; =CH₂ sp²; the methyl branch sp³. (A common slip is to swap the labels of the ethyl CH₂ and the double-bonded C.)

Buta-1,2-diene: H₂C= sp²; the central =C= sp (two double bonds); =CH– sp²; CH₃ sp³.

Exam tip"Explain the hybridization in C₂H₄" [4]: promotion of a 2s electron to 2p (orbital diagram); mixing of one 2s and two 2p orbitals gives three equivalent sp² hybrid orbitals; arranged trigonal planar at 120°; the remaining unhybridized p orbitals on the two carbons overlap sideways to form a π bond.
Advanced noteA lone pair next to a π bond often sits in an unhybridized p orbital so it can join the delocalized system; for example the N in an amide is effectively sp² and planar. You will not usually be tested on this, but it explains why some "expected sp³" atoms are planar.

Typical exam questions and how to answer them

  • "Describe the covalent bond in Cl₂ and how it forms." [2] Electrostatic attraction between the shared pair of electrons and the two positive nuclei; formed by sharing of electrons.
  • "Explain why SiO₂ is a solid but CO₂ is a gas at room temperature." SiO₂: giant covalent network, strong covalent bonds must be broken. CO₂: simple molecules, only weak London forces between molecules must be overcome.
  • "Explain the boiling point trend of the group 15 hydrides." PH₃ < AsH₃ < SbH₃ as London forces increase with number of electrons; NH₃ is anomalously high because of hydrogen bonding.
  • "Predict the shape and bond angle" questions. Always draw the Lewis formula with all lone pairs, count domains, name the shape, give the angle and justify any reduction.
  • "Which species has delocalized electrons?" Look for possible equivalent double-bond positions: O₃, NO₂⁻, NO₃⁻, CO₃²⁻, RCOO⁻, benzene.
  • "Determine the preferred Lewis structure using formal charge." Calculate FC for each atom in each structure; choose the one with FCs closest to zero.
